title: Allocating resources in linear vs iterative schedules
blurb: Categorise resources as re-usable or replenishable, and explain how they are allocated in linear and iterative schedules.
question: Harbour Retail is fitting out a new warehouse using a linear life cycle and building a click-and-collect app iteratively. How should the project manager categorise the resources each needs, and how does allocating them differ between the two schedules?

teach.body: APM groups resources into two categories. RE-USABLE resources (people, equipment, facilities) are available again once a piece of work is done: an engineer finishes one task and moves to the next. REPLENISHABLE, or consumable, resources (materials, money) are used up and must be bought or topped up again. The category matters because it changes the question you plan around: 'how much per period?' for re-usable, 'how much in total, and will it last?' for replenishable.

teach.caption: Resources can also be grouped by skill (electrician, tester, analyst) and as internal (own staff) or external (contractors, suppliers).

rows.label: The training room at head office

teach.note: Hiring makes the scissor lift external, but it is still re-usable: it does not get used up.

teach.body: By SKILL: planning by role or competence (a qualified electrician, a senior tester) shows where scarce skills are the real constraint. INTERNAL versus EXTERNAL: own staff are cheaper and know the organisation but are shared with BAU; contractors and suppliers bring capacity or specialist skills but need contracts, lead times and management. Good categorisation tells the PM which resources need booking early, which need buying, and which need protecting from competing work.

teach.text: Exam traps: calling money or materials 're-usable' (they are replenishable, because they are used up), and calling people 'consumable'. In iterative questions, the wrong answer is usually 'add more people to the time box' or 'extend the time box'. The iterative response is to keep the team and time box fixed and reprioritise the scope.

teach.h: How this comes up in a written answer
items: Name the two APM categories: re-usable (people, equipment, facilities) and replenishable (materials, money).
Explain the difference: available again after use versus used up and reordered.
Linear: assign resources to specific activities, load them, then smooth or level to availability.
Iterative: allocate a stable, dedicated team to each time box; fit scope to its fixed capacity.
Add a benefit: realistic plans, early ordering of materials, protected team capacity.
Re-usable: people, equipment, facilities; free again after use; planned per period.
Replenishable (consumable): materials, money; used up; planned as total quantity.
Also categorise by skill and as internal or external.
Linear: resources assigned to activities, then smoothed or levelled to availability.
Iterative: fixed, stable team per time box; scope chosen to fit capacity.

summary: You can now categorise resources as re-usable or replenishable (and by skill, internal or external) and explain why the category changes how they are planned. You can also contrast allocating resources to activities in a linear schedule with allocating a stable team to time boxes in an iterative one.

A.q: Which of the following is a re-usable resource?
A.why: People are re-usable: once one task is finished they are available for the next.

whyNot.0: Steel is a material: it is used up, so it is replenishable.
whyNot.2: Money is spent and gone, so a budget is replenishable.
whyNot.3: Fuel is consumed, so it is replenishable.

A.q: Which pair are BOTH replenishable (consumable) resources?
A.why: Materials and money are both used up and have to be bought or topped up again.

whyNot.0: Materials are replenishable, but people are re-usable.
whyNot.1: Money is replenishable, but equipment is re-usable.
whyNot.2: Facilities and people are both re-usable.

A.q: In an iterative life cycle, what is normally fixed when allocating resources to a time box?
options: The full scope of the product
The detailed task list for all
A.why: A stable, dedicated team is allocated to each time box, so capacity is fixed and scope is chosen to fit it.

whyNot.1: Scope is what flexes in iterative working, selected by priority from the backlog.
whyNot.2: Detailed tasks are planned time box by time box, not fixed for the whole product up front.
whyNot.3: How many features are delivered depends on what fits the fixed capacity, so it varies.

B.q: What is the key difference between re-usable and replenishable resources?
options: Re-usable ones cost nothing to use
Replenishable ones are always just people
Re-usable ones are free again after use
Replenishable ones can never run out
B.why: Re-usable resources (people, equipment, facilities) become available again when the work is done; replenishable ones are used up.

whyNot.0: Re-usable resources such as staff and hired kit still cost money for the time used.
whyNot.1: People are re-usable; replenishable resources are materials and money.
whyNot.3: The opposite: replenishable resources run out and must be topped up.

B.q: Harbour Retail's warehouse fit-out uses a linear life cycle. How are its resources allocated?
options: As one stable team for each time box
Per activity, then smoothed or levelled
By the team pulling items from a backlog
Only once the deployment phase begins
B.why: In a linear schedule resources are assigned to specific activities on the network or Gantt chart, loaded, then smoothed or levelled to availability.

whyNot.0: Allocating a stable team to each time box is the iterative approach.
whyNot.2: Pulling items from a backlog is how an iterative team selects scope.
whyNot.3: Resources are planned during definition so the baseline is realistic, well before deployment.

B.q: Why does a project manager track the consumption of replenishable resources such as cabling over time?
options: They will be free again next week
They appear on the OBS as team roles
They cannot be bought from any supplier
They are used up and must be reordered
B.why: Consumables run down as work proceeds, so the PM tracks usage to reorder in time and spot waste before supply runs out.

whyNot.0: Becoming free again describes re-usable resources.
whyNot.1: The OBS shows people and organisations, not materials.
whyNot.2: Materials are normally bought from suppliers, which is why lead times matter.

C.q: Midway through a two-week time box, the app team realise they cannot finish all the items they selected. In an iterative approach, what should happen?
options: Add staff to the team for the time box
Extend the time box by a week
Level the schedule to push the date
C.why: The team and time box stay fixed; the product owner agrees which lower-priority items move to a later time box.

whyNot.0: Adding people mid-time box disrupts a stable team and rarely speeds things up immediately.
whyNot.1: Time boxes are fixed; extending them undermines the iterative approach.
whyNot.3: Levelling is a linear scheduling technique; iterative working flexes scope, not dates.

C.q:
Which TWO statements describe allocating resources in a LINEAR schedule?
1) Resources are assigned to specific activities
2) A stable team's capacity sets the scope
3) Loads are smoothed or levelled to availability
4) Scope is pulled from a backlog each time box
C.why: Linear schedules assign resources to activities (1) and then smooth or level the load to what is available (3).

whyNot.0: Statement 2 describes iterative working, where capacity sets scope.
whyNot.3: Statement 3 is linear, but pulling from a backlog (4) is iterative.

C.q: An events company's project budget runs out three weeks before the end, although every team member is still free to work. What does this illustrate?
options: A replenishable resource has run out
The team should have been levelled
The OBS was built from the wrong WBS
C.why: Money is replenishable: once spent it is gone, even though the re-usable resources (the people) are still available.

whyNot.1: The people are free, so the re-usable resource is not over-allocated.
whyNot.2: Levelling resolves clashes over re-usable resources; it does not create more money.
whyNot.3: The problem is a consumed budget, not how responsibilities were mapped.

reteach.title: Running a café
reteach.question: Think about a busy café. What gets used up, what is there again tomorrow, and how does planning a fixed wedding menu differ from planning today's specials?

blocks.h: Used up or there again tomorrow?
blocks.body: The baristas, the coffee machine and the tables are re-usable: after the morning rush they are ready for lunch. Coffee beans, milk, cups and the cash for the day's shopping are replenishable: once used they are gone and must be reordered. Running out of milk stops service just as surely as a barista calling in sick, but you plan for each differently.

blocks.h: A wedding booking versus today's specials

rows.label: Then plan
values: How many dishes they can make

blocks.text: In the iterative café, you do not drag in extra staff halfway through lunch: you keep the shift and cut the specials. That is scope flexing to a fixed team.

explain.body: Re-usable resources (people, equipment, facilities) are available again when a task ends, so you plan how many you need per period. Replenishable resources (materials, money) are consumed, so you plan the total and track it as it runs down.

test.q: A hired excavator finishes digging foundations on Friday. Why is it classed as a re-usable resource?
options: It is paid for out of the budget
It is used up during the work
It is owned by an external firm
It is free again for later work
test.why: Equipment is not consumed by the work, so it is available again for the next task.

whyNot.0: Being paid for does not decide the category; money itself is replenishable.
whyNot.1: Being used up is what makes a resource replenishable.
whyNot.2: Internal or external is a different way of categorising.

explain.body: Grouping by skill shows where scarce competences are the real limit. Internal staff know the organisation but are shared with BAU; external contractors and suppliers add capacity or specialist skills but need contracts, lead times and management.

test.q: A project decides to hire a specialist contractor rather than use its own staff. Which way of categorising resources is being used?
test.why: Choosing between own staff and a contractor is categorising the resource as internal or external.

whyNot.0: Critical and non-critical describe activities on the schedule, not resource sources.
whyNot.1: Both options are people, so both are re-usable; that is not the choice here.
whyNot.3: Fixed and variable are cost types for the budget, not resource categories.

explain.body: Scope is fixed first. Each activity on the network or Gantt chart is given the resources it needs, the loads are totalled per period on a histogram, and the schedule is smoothed or levelled until demand fits availability.

test.q: In a linear schedule, which tool shows whether the resources assigned to activities exceed availability?
test.why: The histogram totals each resource's demand per period against what is available.

whyNot.1: The backlog lists prioritised scope items in iterative working.
whyNot.2: A burn-down chart tracks remaining work in a time box.
whyNot.3: A benefits profile shows when benefits are expected.

explain.body: A stable, dedicated, cross-functional team is allocated to each time box, so capacity is fixed and known. The product owner prioritises the backlog and the team selects the items that fit. If more work appears, priorities change: not the team or the deadline.

items.label: people, same team every time box

test.q: In iterative working, what is adjusted to match the fixed capacity of the team?
test.why: Team and time are fixed, so the scope taken into each time box is chosen to fit the capacity.

whyNot.0: Time boxes are fixed in length.
whyNot.1: The team is kept stable so its capacity is predictable.
whyNot.3: Deadlines are protected; scope flexes instead.
